subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Subject: Your first month, specifically
Hi Deepak,
In our check-in yesterday you said you "just got lucky" with the vendor report. I didn't argue then, but I want to put this in writing, because I don't think it was luck.
Three things you did:
1. You noticed the two suppliers were using different units and converted them before anyone else caught it. That saved us a wrong order.
2. Your summary on page one was four lines. Our director read it in the lift and forwarded it without edits. That almost never happens.
3. When you weren't sure about the warehouse codes, you asked Meera instead of guessing.
I know a new job makes everyone feel like a fake; I felt it for a year. But these are facts, not compliments. Keep this email, and read it again the next time you think you don't belong here.
Payal

qa.q: What did Deepak notice about the two suppliers?
qa.a: That they were using different units, which Deepak converted before anyone else caught it.

qa.q: Why did Payal decide to put the praise in writing?
qa.a: Payal was concerned that Deepak was dismissing real work as luck and, having felt like a fake in a new job once, wanted to give facts Deepak could keep.

qa.q: Why is Payal's praise more likely to be believed than a quick "good job"?
qa.a: It names specific actions and results, like the unit conversion and the four-line summary, which a doubting mind cannot easily dismiss.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel reading the email?
qa.a: Deepak may feel surprised and reassured, seeing concrete proof that the good result was not luck.

grounding: Shows a manager giving a doubting newcomer specific, honest praise that names exactly what was done, so it cannot be brushed off as vague.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: "Kamal, sit. You're making that face again, the one that says 'it was just luck'. I know it well, because I wore it for years. At twenty-four I joined the newspaper in Pune as a junior sub-editor. In my second month I wrote a headline for the flood story that the editor pinned on the notice board. Everyone congratulated me. And what did I say? 'Oh, the story was so strong, anyone could have done it.' When I was moved up to the city page, I told myself they were short of people. But one small spelling mistake in a caption, and I cried in the ladies' room, sure that now they would see the truth about me. Praise went in one ear and out the other. Mistakes, I kept like a diary. Your Irawati aaji took twenty years to learn to keep both."

qa.q: What did young Irawati write that was pinned on the notice board?
qa.a: A headline for the flood story.

qa.q: How did young Irawati feel about the caption mistake?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and frightened, sure that now they would see the truth about her.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have helped young Irawati?
qa.a: Keeping the praise, like the pinned headline and the move to the city page, as carefully as the mistakes, instead of explaining it away.

qa.q: How might the editor have seen young Irawati's work?
qa.a: The editor clearly valued it, pinning the headline and later moving her up, even while she believed it was luck.

grounding: Shows a young worker crediting luck or the story for every success while treating one small error as proof of being found out.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Tuesday.
Another planning meeting, another hour of saying nothing. Naveen talked for ten minutes about the new dashboard like he had invented dashboards. Everyone nodded. I had an idea about the filter problem, a good one I think, but I kept imagining him raising one eyebrow, so I stayed quiet and doodled boxes in my notebook.
Everyone there looks so sure. Meanwhile inside me it's all what if I'm wrong, what if it's obvious, what if it's stupid. Comparing my insides to their outsides, Didi calls it.
The worst part: at the end the manager said, "Saurabh, anything to add?" and I said, "No, all good." Then she gave the filter work to Naveen. Of course. Why wouldn't she? I've been invisible for three months. Now I'm annoyed at myself for being invisible and at them for not seeing me, both at once.

qa.q: What did Saurabh doodle during the meeting?
qa.a: Boxes in a notebook.

qa.q: What feelings does Saurabh have at the end of the meeting?
qa.a: Saurabh feels annoyed at being invisible and frustrated with the others for not noticing, both at once.

qa.q: What small step could help Saurabh at the next meeting?
qa.a: Saurabh could note the idea beforehand and share it early, or send it to the manager afterwards, so silence stops feeding the belief.

qa.q: How might the manager see Saurabh after three months?
qa.a: The manager likely sees someone with nothing to add, so the filter work went to Naveen, not knowing Saurabh had a good idea.

grounding: Shows a newcomer comparing inner doubts with colleagues' outward confidence and staying silent, which makes them less visible and feeds the doubt.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Hi Harsha,
A short note after today's review. I noticed you didn't say anything in the meeting again, and I also noticed that the fix everyone was praising, the retry logic in the billing service, came from your code on Monday. I made sure to tell the team lead that afterwards, with your name on it.
Can I tell you something? In my first year here, I didn't speak in a single review for four months. I was sure everyone knew more than me. A senior called Latha asked me directly, "Pradeep, what do you think?" and waited. That one question changed a lot.
So here's my version: in Thursday's meeting, I'm going to ask you to explain the retry logic for two minutes. You know it better than anyone. If that feels like too much, tell me, and we'll do it together.
Pradeep

qa.q: Whose code contained the retry logic everyone praised?
qa.a: Harsha's code from Monday.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep want to help Harsha speak up?
qa.a: Pradeep remembers feeling unsure and silent for four months, and cares that Harsha's good work is going unheard.

qa.q: Which parts of Pradeep's plan help Harsha find a voice?
qa.a: Giving specific credit to the team lead, sharing Pradeep's own silent first year, and inviting a two-minute explanation with an offer to do it together.

qa.q: What might Harsha feel reading this note?
qa.a: Harsha may feel seen and a bit nervous, but encouraged by the credit and the offer of support.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague noticing a capable, silent newcomer and helping by giving specific credit, sharing their own early doubts and inviting their view.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: Six months into the job, I started a document called "Facts". It was Varun's idea. He had heard me say, for the third time, "I have no idea why they hired me," and said, "Pallavi, write down what you've actually done. Not how you feel. What happened." So I did. Shipped the onboarding flow, two days early. Client email: "clearest demo we've had." Fixed the invoice bug nobody else could find. Asked for the analytics project and got it. Last Thursday, after a rough review, the old thought came roaring back: you're a fraud, they'll find out. Instead of arguing with the feeling, I opened the document and read it slowly, like evidence in a court case. The feeling didn't vanish. But the thought looked weaker next to eleven facts. I added a twelfth that night.

qa.q: What did Pallavi call the document?
qa.a: "Facts".

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel after reading the document last Thursday?
qa.a: The anxious feeling didn't vanish, but Pallavi felt steadier, with the fraud thought looking weaker next to eleven facts.

qa.q: Why does reading the list work better than trying to feel confident?
qa.a: It tests the thought against facts a doubting mind can accept, instead of fighting a feeling with another feeling.

qa.q: What might Varun have noticed that led to the idea?
qa.a: Varun heard Pallavi say "I have no idea why they hired me" three times and was likely concerned enough to suggest a practical fix.

grounding: Shows a person keeping a list of finished work and good feedback and reading it when doubt spikes, testing the thought against facts.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: A year after joining the farm advisory office in Barabanki, Indu still didn't know every seed variety by name, and she no longer pretended to. When a farmer asked about a new pest on his okra, she said, "I'm not sure. Let me check with the district lab and come to your field on Thursday," and she did. On Monday a new trainee, Vijay, arrived: pressed shirt, anxious eyes, nodding at every term. At lunch under the neem tree, Indu shared her tiffin and said, "In my first month I thought 'soil health card' was some kind of ID. Nobody knows everything here. Ask me anything." Vijay laughed, surprised, and asked three questions in a row. Walking back, Indu realised she had answered two of them easily. She felt, quietly, that she belonged.

qa.q: What did Indu tell the farmer about the new pest?
qa.a: That she wasn't sure and would check with the district lab and come to his field on Thursday.

qa.q: How did Indu feel walking back after lunch?
qa.a: She felt quietly settled, a sense that she belonged, after answering two of Vijay's questions easily.

qa.q: Why does Indu's openness about not knowing help Vijay?
qa.a: Sharing her own early mistake makes not knowing feel normal, so Vijay can ask questions instead of nodding.

qa.q: What is lunch under the neem tree like for Vijay?
qa.a: Vijay arrives anxious but laughs in surprise and feels safe enough to ask three questions.

grounding: Shows a worker whose confidence has grown with competence, accepting not knowing everything and helping the next newcomer, which deepens belonging.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
subtype: Stage 1: The news and the glow [Actor]
passage: The email arrived at 4:12 p.m. on a Wednesday: "Please join me in congratulating Nirmala on her new role as Team Lead, Payments Platform." Nirmala read it three times at her desk in the Hitech City office, then went to the washroom just to smile at herself in the mirror. Six years of night deployments, weekend bug fixes and quietly training every new joiner. Mridul, her desk neighbour, had already stuck a paper crown on her monitor. By evening her phone wouldn't stop: Amma sending a string of flower emojis, her brother calling from Dubai, the old college group filling up with "Boss lady!" At dinner Appa told the whole family, twice, "She earned it." Lying awake that night, Nirmala thought: yes, I did.

qa.q: When did the email arrive?
qa.a: At 4:12 p.m. on a Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Nirmala feel when reading the email?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, slipping off to the mirror just to smile after six years of effort.

qa.q: What could help Nirmala carry this pride well into the new role?
qa.a: Enjoying the moment while remembering the colleagues and habits, like training new joiners, that got her here.

qa.q: How does Mridul seem to feel about the promotion?
qa.a: Mridul seems happy for her, sticking a paper crown on her monitor before she was even back.

grounding: Shows a well-liked engineer made team lead, proud and validated after years of work, with family and friends celebrating the earned reward.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Manager's note, one-to-one prep, Friday.
Rashmi has been team lead for three months, and delivery is strong. But I've noticed a change. In Tuesday's design review she said "As I decided back in March" three times. When Karan questioned her caching choice, she smiled, said "Let's trust experience here," and moved on. The juniors now wait for her view before speaking, and she seems to enjoy it. When I thanked the team for the release, she looked slightly put out that her name wasn't first. Three months ago she credited the juniors before herself. I don't think she sees it yet. At our one-to-one on Monday I'll praise the results, then ask how she makes room for disagreement, and share Karan's point about caching, which was a good one.
Sudha

qa.q: What phrase did Rashmi repeat three times in the design review?
qa.a: "As I decided back in March."

qa.q: What does Rashmi's reaction to the team thanks suggest about how she now feels?
qa.a: She seems a little hurt and put out, expecting praise to come to her first, as if it were now her due.

qa.q: What turning point does the manager plan for Monday?
qa.a: Praising the results but asking how Rashmi makes room for disagreement, and sharing Karan's good point about caching.

qa.q: What might Karan feel after being brushed off?
qa.a: Karan probably feels dismissed and frustrated, since a good point was waved away with "trust experience".

grounding: Shows a new lead quoting past decisions, enjoying deference and coming to expect praise, as noticed by the manager.
